title: Floating point in JavaScript: binary fractions, rounding, and precision limits
description: Why `0.1 + 0.2` isn't `0.3`, why `toFixed` sometimes rounds the wrong way, where negative zero comes from, what happens above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, and why adding the same numbers in a different order can change the total. Every answer follows from IEEE 754 and ECMA-262.

questions.title: What does `0.1 + 0.2` evaluate to in JavaScript?

images.alt: 0.1 written out in binary as a chip sequence: 0001, then 1001 repeating forever, with a dashed cut line marking where the double's 52 mantissa bits stop and the value rounds up to 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625.
images.caption: `0.1` and `0.2` both round up when stored, which is why their sum overshoots `0.3`.

questions.explanation:
`0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`.

Neither input is exact. As doubles, `0.1` is really `0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625` and `0.2` is really `0.200000000000000011102230246251565404236316680908203125`.

Both round up when the parser reads them, so their sum comes out a little high. The nearest double to that sum is `0.3000000000000000444089209850062616169452667236328125`, which prints as `0.30000000000000004`. The literal `0.3` parses to a different double, `0.299999999999999988897769753748434595763683319091796875`. The bit patterns differ, so `===` returns `false`.

`toFixed(20)` shows the digits that printing normally hides:

```js
(0.1).toFixed(20);       // "0.10000000000000000555"  rounded up
(0.2).toFixed(20);       // "0.20000000000000001110"  rounded up
(0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(20); // "0.30000000000000004441"
(0.3).toFixed(20);       // "0.29999999999999998890"  rounded down
```

Floats aren't random. The same inputs always give the same result. The rounding just happens earlier than most people expect, when the literal is parsed.
questions.references:
- [0.30000000000000004.com, the same result in 100+ languages](https://0.30000000000000004.com/)
- [Wikipedia: Double-precision floating-point format](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-precision_floating-point_format)
- [float.exposed, the bits of `0.1` laid out](https://float.exposed/0x3fb999999999999a)

questions.title: Why can a double hold `0.5` exactly but not `0.1`?

images.alt: The 64 bits of a double laid out as a bit grid: 1 sign bit, an 11-bit biased exponent, and a 52-bit mantissa, with the formula value equals minus one to the sign times 1.mantissa times 2 to the exponent minus 1023.
images.caption: The exponent moves the binary point. The mantissa has a fixed number of bits, and `1/10` doesn't fit in them.

images.alt: 0.1 written out in binary as a chip sequence: 0001, then 1001 repeating forever, with a dashed cut line marking where the double's 52 mantissa bits stop and the value rounds up to 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625.
images.caption: `1/10` repeats forever in binary, the same way `1/3` repeats forever in decimal.

options.text: `1/2` is a finite binary fraction. `1/10` has a factor of 5 in the denominator, so in base 2 it repeats forever and has to be cut off.
Doubles carry about 15 decimal digits, and `0.1` needs 16 to write down.
`0.1` is stored exactly. The error only appears once you add it to something else.
The engine keeps small decimals as strings and loses digits when it converts them to numbers.

questions.explanation:
A double stores `sign × significand × 2^exponent`, which is a binary fraction. A number fits exactly only if its denominator, in lowest terms, is a power of two.

`0.5 = 1/2`, `0.25 = 1/4`, and `0.75 = 3/4` all fit. `0.1 = 1/10 = 1/(2 × 5)` doesn't, because of the factor of 5. In binary it's `0.0001100110011…`, repeating forever, just like `1/3` in decimal. The engine keeps 53 bits of significand and rounds the rest.

`toFixed(20)` shows the difference:

```js
(0.5).toFixed(20);  // "0.50000000000000000000"  exact
(0.25).toFixed(20); // "0.25000000000000000000"  exact
(0.75).toFixed(20); // "0.75000000000000000000"  exact
(0.1).toFixed(20);  // "0.10000000000000000555"  not exact
```

The stored `0.1` is as close as a double can get, within about 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁸.

The number of decimal digits doesn't matter. `0.1` has one digit and can't be stored exactly, while `0.5`, `0.0625`, and `1048576.5` are longer and exact.
questions.references:
- [David Goldberg: *What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic*](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_goldberg.html)
- [Wikipedia: Double-precision floating-point format](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-precision_floating-point_format)

questions.title: Which of these strict comparisons evaluates to `true`?
questions.explanation:
Only `0.1 + 0.3 === 0.4` is true. Here's what each sum actually gives:

```js
0.1 + 0.2; // 0.30000000000000004
0.1 + 0.3; // 0.4                 <- exact
0.1 + 0.7; // 0.7999999999999999
0.2 + 0.4; // 0.6000000000000001
```

People often remember `0.1 + 0.7 === 0.8` as a pair that works. It's false.

Some tenths do add exactly. `0.1 + 0.6`, `0.3 + 0.4`, and `0.4 + 0.5` all match their literal. There's no easy pattern, because the result depends on three separate roundings: the two operands when parsed, the sum after the addition, and the literal on the right when parsed.

So don't try to memorize the safe pairs. Just don't use `===` on computed floats. If your code is correct only because a rounding happened to go one way, a different input will break it.

questions.title: How far apart are `0.1 + 0.2` and `0.3` on the double number line?

images.alt: Four number-line panels showing the gap between representable doubles widening with magnitude: near 0.3 the ULP is about 5.6 times 10 to the minus 17, near 2 to the 52 the ULP is 1, at 2 to the 53 the ULP becomes 2 and 2 to the 53 plus 1 collides with 2 to the 53, and by 2 to the 60 the ULP is 256.
images.caption: Near 0.3, doubles are about 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ apart. `0.1 + 0.2` lands one step above `0.3`.

options.text: Exactly one ULP. `0.1 + 0.2` is the very next representable double above `0.3`, with nothing in between.
About 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁷, which is roughly 250 ULPs at that magnitude.
Zero. They are the same double, and only `String()` renders them differently.
Exactly one `Number.EPSILON`, i.e. 2.22 × 10⁻¹⁶.

questions.explanation:
Read the 8 bytes of each double as a 64-bit integer, and the two bit patterns are consecutive:

```js
0.3       -> 0x3fd3333333333333
0.1 + 0.2 -> 0x3fd3333333333334
```

They're one ULP (unit in the last place) apart. At this size one ULP is 2⁻⁵⁴ ≈ 5.551 × 10⁻¹⁷, which is why `0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3` gives `5.551115123125783e-17`. That's a single step, not a buildup of error.

So the addition was as accurate as a double allows. It landed one step away, the smallest possible difference between two doubles, and that's still enough to make `===` fail.

One ULP isn't the same as `Number.EPSILON`. `Number.EPSILON` is the ULP at 1, which is 2⁻⁵². That's four times the ULP near 0.3, and far smaller than the ULP near 10⁷.
questions.references:
- [Wikipedia: Unit in the last place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_in_the_last_place)
- [float.exposed, inspect these bit patterns yourself](https://float.exposed/0x3fd3333333333333)

questions.title: Why does `String(0.1)` print `"0.1"` while `String(0.1 + 0.2)` prints all 17 digits?
questions.description:
Both values are inexact, but only one of them looks that way.

```js
String(0.1);       // "0.1"
String(0.1 + 0.2); // "0.30000000000000004"
```

options.text: ECMA-262 prints the shortest decimal string that parses back to the same double. `"0.1"` round-trips. For the sum, nothing shorter than 17 digits does.
`0.1` is stored exactly and the sum is not, so only the sum has extra digits to show.
The engine caches the source text of numeric literals and replays it, while computed values get rebuilt from the bits.
`String()` truncates at the first run of zeros, and the sum has no run of zeros to truncate at.

questions.explanation:
Both values are inexact. The difference comes from how numbers are printed.

ECMA-262 converts a number to a string by finding the shortest decimal that parses back to the same double. You can check the candidates yourself:

```js
Number("0.1") === 0.1;                       // true  -> 1 digit is enough
Number("0.3") === 0.1 + 0.2;                 // false -> not enough
Number("0.30000000000000004") === 0.1 + 0.2; // true  -> 17 digits needed
```

`"0.1"` is the shortest string that parses back to the stored double, so that's what you see, even though the stored value is `0.1000000000000000055511…`. The sum is one ULP away from `0.3`, so any shorter string would parse as `0.3`. The printer needs 17 significant digits to tell them apart.

This means `console.log` hides small errors by design. A value that prints as `0.1` isn't exactly one tenth. To see the real value, use `toFixed(20)` or look at the bits.

questions.title: What does `(0.1).toFixed(20)` return?

images.alt: 0.1 written out in binary as a chip sequence: 0001, then 1001 repeating forever, with a dashed cut line marking where the double's 52 mantissa bits stop and the value rounds up to 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625.
images.caption: Every double is a finite binary fraction, so the double nearest `0.1` does end. It just needs 53 bits.

questions.explanation:
Ask for more digits than the shortest round-trip string, and you see the stored value:

```js
(0.1).toFixed(20); // "0.10000000000000000555"
```

The exact value of the double nearest `0.1` is

```text
0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625
```

and it ends. Every double is a finite binary fraction, so its decimal expansion is finite too, though it can be long. `toFixed(20)` shows the first 20 decimal places. Modern engines accept 0 to 100 digits, so `(0.1).toFixed(100)` shows all of it.

Notice the direction. The stored value is slightly above one tenth, which is why `0.1 + 0.2` overshoots `0.3` instead of falling short.

questions.title: What string does `(1.005).toFixed(2)` return?
questions.explanation:
It's `"1.00"`, not `"1.01"`.

This gets reported as a rounding bug, but the problem is storage. `1.005` can't be stored as a double:

```js
(1.005).toFixed(20); // "1.00499999999999989342"
```

The exact stored value is `1.00499999999999989341858963598497211933135986328125`, just below the halfway point. There's no tie to break, and `toFixed` rounds correctly. It simply got a slightly smaller number than the one you typed.

`(2.675).toFixed(2)` gives `"2.67"` and `(1.045).toFixed(2)` gives `"1.04"` for the same reason. That doesn't mean it always rounds down. `(1.235).toFixed(2)` gives `"1.24"`, because that literal is stored slightly above its halfway point. Which way a given price rounds depends on how the parser happened to store it.

questions.title: Which result shows that `toFixed` doesn't use banker's rounding, given that `(1.005).toFixed(2)` returns `"1.00"`?
questions.description: Banker's rounding (round half to even) would also turn a true tie at `1.005` into `1.00`, because `0` is even. So that result alone can't tell you which rule `toFixed` uses.

options.text: `(0.5).toFixed(0)` is `"1"` and `(2.5).toFixed(0)` is `"3"`, so real ties round away from zero, never to even.
`(1.045).toFixed(2)` is `"1.04"`, and `4` is even, which is what banker's rounding would give.
`Math.round(2.5)` is `3`, and `toFixed` calls `Math.round` internally.
`toFixed` returns a string, and banker's rounding is only defined for numeric results.

questions.explanation:
You need a real tie. Halves are exact in binary, so `0.5` and `2.5` are stored exactly, and you can see the tie rule directly:

```js
(0.5).toFixed(0); // "1"   banker's would give "0"
(2.5).toFixed(0); // "3"   banker's would give "2"
(1.5).toFixed(0); // "2"
```

ECMA-262 defines it this way: pick the integer *n* that minimizes `|n / 10^f − x|`, and if there are two, pick the larger one. That's round half up on the magnitude (half away from zero), the opposite of round half to even.

So `(1.005).toFixed(2)` returning `"1.00"` isn't a tie-breaking decision, because the stored value isn't a tie. The difference matters because the two causes need different fixes. You fix a tie-breaking problem by choosing a rounding mode. You fix a storage problem only by not storing the value in binary.

Negative numbers work a little differently. `toFixed` removes the sign first and rounds the magnitude, so `(-0.5).toFixed(0)` is `"-1"`. `Math.round` rounds ties toward positive infinity, so `Math.round(-0.5)` is `-0`.

questions.title: What do these two ways of rounding `1.005` to two decimals print in the same runtime?

options.text: `"1.00"` and `"1.01"`, so the two APIs disagree.
`"1.00"` and `"1.00"`, because both see the same stored value and both round down.
`"1.01"` and `"1.01"`, because both apply half-away-from-zero to the literal.
`"1.00"` and `"1.005"`, because `Intl` ignores `maximumFractionDigits` for exact literals.

questions.explanation:
They disagree in every major engine, including V8 (Node, Chrome) and JavaScriptCore (Bun, Safari):

```js
(1.005).toFixed(2); // "1.00"
fmt.format(1.005);  // "1.01"
fmt.format(2.675);  // "2.68"   (toFixed gives "2.67")
```

The two APIs round different values. `toFixed` is defined on the exact binary value `1.00499999999999989…`, which is below halfway. `Intl` formatters, which use ICU in practice, first convert the double to its shortest round-trip decimal, the string `"1.005"`, and round that. That's an exact tie, so it rounds up.

Which one is "right" matters less than the fact that they differ. Both claim to round to two decimals, and they return different amounts of money. Pick one and use it everywhere. If you compute a total with `toFixed` and display it with `Intl`, sooner or later you'll be a cent off, and you'll find out from a reconciliation report.

questions.title: What does `Math.round(1.005 * 100) / 100` evaluate to?
questions.explanation:
It returns `1`, which prints as `"1"`. That's arguably worse than the `"1.00"` you were trying to fix.

Step by step:

```js
1.005 * 100;                    // 100.49999999999999
Math.round(100.49999999999999); // 100
100 / 100;                      // 1
```

Multiplying by 100 doesn't undo the storage error. `1.005` was already slightly too small, and the multiplication rounds again, so the product lands just under `100.5`.

This happens with lots of values. `0.07 * 100` is `7.000000000000001`, `1.13 * 100` is `112.99999999999999`, and `4.35 * 100` is `434.99999999999994`. `Math.round` fixes those three, which is what makes the trick risky: it passes your tests and fails on other inputs.

The real fix is to never turn the value into a binary float. Parse `"1.005"` into integer minor units (like cents) or a decimal type as soon as it enters your code.
questions.references:
- [MDN: Math.round()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Math/round)
- [David Goldberg: *What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic*](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_goldberg.html)

questions.title: Which of these expressions evaluate to `true`?

options.text: `Object.is(-0, 0)`
`[0].includes(-0)`
`new Set([0, -0]).size === 1`
`JSON.stringify(-0) === "0"`

questions.explanation:
JavaScript has three ways to compare values, and `-0` is where they disagree.

```js
-0 === 0;              // true
Object.is(-0, 0);      // false
[0].includes(-0);      // true
new Set([0, -0]).size; // 1
1 / -0 === 1 / 0;      // false
JSON.stringify(-0);    // "0"
```

| Algorithm | Used by | `+0` vs `-0` | `NaN` vs `NaN` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strict Equality | `===`, `!==` | same | different |
| SameValueZero | `includes`, `Set`, `Map` keys | same | same |
| SameValue | `Object.is` | different | same |

The table covers four of the six. `-0 === 0` is `true` and `Object.is(-0, 0)` is `false`. The collection methods treat the two zeros as equal, like `===`, but treat `NaN` as equal to itself, like `Object.is`.

`1 / -0 === 1 / 0` is `false` because it becomes `-Infinity === Infinity`. Division is where the sign of a zero starts to matter.

`JSON.stringify(-0)` is `"0"`, so serializing loses the sign. Parsing keeps it, though: `Object.is(JSON.parse("-0"), -0)` is `true`.

You can run into this in React. `useState` uses `Object.is` to decide whether to skip a render, so changing state from `0` to `-0` causes a re-render even though `===` says they're equal.

questions.title: Which of these expressions produces `-0`?
questions.description: Each one starts with a negative number or a zero. Only one keeps the minus sign in the result.

options.text: `Math.round(-0.2)`
`Math.abs(-0)`
`Math.max(-0, 0)`

questions.explanation:
`Math.round(-0.2)` is `-0`. You can check with `Object.is(Math.round(-0.2), -0)`, which returns `true`.

IEEE 754 says that when rounding gives zero, the result keeps the operand's sign. So any small negative number that rounds to zero gives you `-0`:

```js
Math.round(-0.2);  // -0
Math.round(-0.5);  // -0   ties round toward +Infinity
Math.ceil(-0.5);   // -0
Math.trunc(-0.5);  // -0
Math.sign(-0);     // -0
-1 % 1;            // -0
0 * -1;            // -0
Number("-0");      // -0
```

The other three give `+0`. `Math.abs` always clears the sign. `Math.max(-0, 0)` is defined to return `+0` (and `Math.min(0, -0)` returns `-0`). `0 - 0` is `+0` in the default rounding mode.

So you don't have to type `-0` to get it. Ordinary rounding of small negative numbers produces it, and you won't notice, because `String(-0)` is `"0"`.

questions.title: Why does this trend indicator say "falling" for a metric that barely moved?

options.text: `Math.round(-0.2)` is `-0`, and `1 / -0` is `-Infinity`, which is less than zero.
`Math.round(-0.2)` is `-1`, so the slope is `-1`.
`1 / 0` is `NaN`, and `NaN < 0` evaluates to `true`.
`Math.round` throws on negative arguments below `0.5`, and the caught value defaults to `-1`.

questions.explanation:
`Math.round(-0.2)` is `-0`, and then:

```js
1 / -0;         // -Infinity
-Infinity < 0;  // true  -> "falling"
```

Division is the usual place `-0` escapes. It turns the hidden sign of a zero into an infinity with a visible sign. Everything before that point hides it: `-0 === 0` is `true`, `-0 < 0` is `false`, `String(-0)` is `"0"`, and debuggers usually show `0`.

The other two numeric options are simply wrong. `Math.round(-0.2)` isn't `-1`, because `-0.2` is closer to zero. And `1 / 0` is `Infinity`, not `NaN`. Only `0 / 0` gives `NaN`.

To fix it, test what you actually care about, `delta < 0`, instead of getting the sign through a division. If you really need to detect negative zero, `Object.is(x, -0)` is the only reliable check.

questions.title: What do `(-0).toFixed(1)` and `(-0.04).toFixed(1)` return?
questions.description:
Dashboards often show `-0.0%`. Only one of these two calls produces it.

```js
(-0).toFixed(1);    // ?
(-0.04).toFixed(1); // ?
```
questions.explanation:
Surprisingly, the `-0.0%` on your dashboard doesn't come from `-0`.

`toFixed` first checks `x < 0`. If that's true, it writes `"-"` and continues with `-x`. But `-0 < 0` is `false`, since comparison treats the two zeros as equal. So `-0` never gets a minus sign, and `(-0).toFixed(1)` is `"0.0"`.

`-0.04` really is less than zero, so it gets the sign. Then the magnitude rounds to `0.0`, and you get `"-0.0"`. The same happens with `(-0.4).toFixed(0)`, which gives `"-0"`.

The cause is a small negative number that passes the sign check and then rounds to zero. Check the formatted value, not the input:

```js
const s = value.toFixed(1);
const display = Number(s) === 0 ? (0).toFixed(1) : s;
```

questions.title: What is the value of `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`?
questions.description: Type the integer, with no separators.

images.alt: The 64 bits of a double laid out as a bit grid: 1 sign bit, an 11-bit biased exponent, and a 52-bit mantissa, with the formula value equals minus one to the sign times 1.mantissa times 2 to the exponent minus 1023.
images.caption: 52 stored mantissa bits plus 1 implicit leading bit give 53 bits of precision, enough to count every integer from 0 to 2⁵³.

questions.explanation:
It's `9007199254740991`, or 2⁵³ − 1.

A double stores 52 bits of significand plus one implicit leading bit, so it has 53 bits of precision. That's enough to represent every integer from 0 to 2⁵³ exactly.

```js
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER === 2 ** 53 - 1; // true
Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53 - 1);       // true
Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53);           // false
```

Larger integers still exist as doubles, but they're more than 1 apart.

So where does the limit matter? `Date.now()` in milliseconds stays safe until about the year 285,000, so timestamps are fine. Database `BIGINT` primary keys, Twitter and Discord snowflake IDs, and nanosecond counters are not.

questions.title: `2 ** 53` is stored exactly, so why is `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` one less than it?

images.alt: The 64 bits of a double laid out as a bit grid: 1 sign bit, an 11-bit biased exponent, and a 52-bit mantissa, with the formula value equals minus one to the sign times 1.mantissa times 2 to the exponent minus 1023.
images.caption: 52 stored bits plus 1 implicit leading bit give 53 bits of precision. The "only 52 bits" answer forgets the leading bit.

images.alt: Four number-line panels showing the gap between representable doubles widening with magnitude: near 0.3 the ULP is about 5.6 times 10 to the minus 17, near 2 to the 52 the ULP is 1, at 2 to the 53 the ULP becomes 2 and 2 to the 53 plus 1 collides with 2 to the 53, and by 2 to the 60 the ULP is 256.
images.caption: At `2 ** 53`, neighbouring doubles are 2 apart, so `2 ** 53 + 1` rounds onto `2 ** 53`.

options.text: Because `2 ** 53 + 1` rounds down to `2 ** 53`, so that double no longer stands for exactly one integer.
Because the significand holds only 52 bits, and `2 ** 53` needs 53 of them.
Because array indices are capped at `2 ** 53 - 1`, and the constant was defined to match.
Because `2 ** 53` is reserved as a sentinel and comparisons against it are unspecified.

questions.explanation:
"Safe" means more than "representable". ECMA-262 defines a safe integer as one that's exactly representable and that no other integer rounds to. `2 ** 53` passes the first test and fails the second:

```js
2 ** 53 === 2 ** 53 + 1;           // true  <- two integers, one double
Number.isInteger(2 ** 53);         // true
Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53);     // false
Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53 - 1); // true
```

At 2⁵³ the gap between neighbouring doubles becomes 2, so 2⁵³ and 2⁵³ + 1 end up with the same bits. The odd value is exactly halfway, and round half to even sends it to the even neighbour.

2⁵³ itself is still exact. The problem is that when you see that value, you can't tell which integer produced it. And `x + 1 === x` becomes true, which breaks loops, counters, and uniqueness checks.

The "only 52 bits" answer forgets the implicit leading 1. 52 stored bits plus 1 implicit bit is 53 bits of precision, which is why 2⁵³ fits.

questions.title: Which statements about doubles above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` are true?
questions.description: `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is about the spacing between doubles, not the largest number.

images.alt: Four number-line panels showing the gap between representable doubles widening with magnitude: near 0.3 the ULP is about 5.6 times 10 to the minus 17, near 2 to the 52 the ULP is 1, at 2 to the 53 the ULP becomes 2 and 2 to the 53 plus 1 collides with 2 to the 53, and by 2 to the 60 the ULP is 256.
images.caption: By `2 ** 60`, neighbouring doubles are 256 apart. Each one is exact, but there are far fewer of them.

options.text: `2 ** 60` is stored exactly, with zero error.
The gap between neighbouring doubles doubles at every power of two.
`Number.isInteger(2 ** 53 + 1)` is `true`.
`Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 60)` is `true`.
Integers above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` become approximations, and none of them is exact.

questions.explanation:
Doubles go up to about 1.8 × 10³⁰⁸. 2⁵³ is where you run out of precision, not range.

```js
2 ** 60 === Number(2n ** 60n);  // true   exact, no error
(2 ** 60 + 256) - 2 ** 60;      // 256    the gap up there
(2 ** 53 + 2) - 2 ** 53;        // 2      the gap here
Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 60);  // false  exact, but not alone
```

Every power of two is exact at any size, because it's a single bit. What changes is the ULP. Below 2⁵³ the gap is at most 1, so every integer has its own double. At 2⁵³ the gap is 2, at 2⁵⁴ it's 4, and by 2⁶⁰ it's 256. So 2⁶⁰ is exact, and 2⁶⁰ + 1 has no double at all.

`Number.isInteger(2 ** 53 + 1)` is `true` because of that rounding. The expression evaluates to `2 ** 53`, which is an integer. That's the catch with `Number.isInteger`: it tells you the value is a whole number, not that it's the number you meant. Use `Number.isSafeInteger` when that matters.

questions.title: What does `JSON.parse('{"id": 1234567890123456789}').id` return?

options.text: It throws a `SyntaxError`, because the literal exceeds `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`.

questions.explanation:
You get `1234567890123456800`. The last three digits changed with no error, no warning, and no clamping to `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. `JSON.parse` produces a double, and the nearest double to that integer is 11 away.

This is why Twitter added `id_str` next to `id` in its API. The numeric field was unusable from JavaScript, so every ID was also sent as a string. A snowflake ID packs a millisecond timestamp, a machine ID, and a sequence counter into 64 bits. The low bits tell apart IDs created in the same millisecond, and those are the first bits a double drops.

The bug is hard to spot because the result still looks like a valid ID. Your code passes it around and sends it back to the server, where it points to a different row or to nothing.

Fixes, best first: have the API send IDs as strings, parse with a `BigInt`-aware reviver, or otherwise never let the value become a `Number`.

```js
// The value is intact in the source text. It only dies on conversion.
JSON.parse(text, (k, v, ctx) => (k === "id" ? BigInt(ctx.source) : v));
```

questions.title: Summing the same array forwards and backwards gives two different totals. What are they?

options.text: Both `10000000001000000`. Only the intermediate values differ.

questions.explanation:
Forwards, all million ones are lost. Backwards, they're kept. The totals differ by 1,000,000, far more than any rounding error.

Forwards, the running total starts at `1e16`, where doubles are 2 apart. Adding `1` lands exactly halfway between two doubles, and round half to even sends it back to `1e16`:

```js
1e16 + 1 === 1e16; // true
```

That happens a million times, and the total never changes.

Backwards, the ones add up first. They're small and exact, so they reach `1000000` before `1e16` is added. `10000000001000000` is even, so it's representable, and nothing is lost.

This is what people mean when they say floating-point addition isn't associative. Here's a smaller example:

```js
(0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3; // 0.6000000000000001
0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3); // 0.6
```

It's also why a parallel or vectorized sum can differ from a serial one on the same input. The reduction changes the grouping, and the grouping decides the result.
questions.references:
- [Wikipedia: Kahan summation algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahan_summation_algorithm)
- [David Goldberg: *What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic*](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_goldberg.html)

questions.title: Which summation algorithm carries a running compensation term to recover the low-order bits lost at each addition?
questions.description: It's named after the numerical analyst who published it in 1965. It's also called compensated summation.

questions.title: In Kahan summation, what does `c` hold after the line `c = (t - sum) - y`?

options.text: The part of `y` that was lost when it was added to `sum`, meaning the bits that fell off the end.
The running total so far, kept at higher precision as a backup.
The exact difference between the true sum and the float sum over the whole array.
Zero, unless the input contains `NaN` or `Infinity`.

questions.explanation:
`(t - sum)` is how much of `y` actually made it into the total. Subtract the `y` you meant to add, and what's left is the shortfall, the low bits dropped when `sum + y` was rounded.

Walk through the extreme case. Start with `sum = 1e16` and `y = 1`. `t = 1e16 + 1` rounds to `1e16`, so `t - sum` is `0` and nothing was added. That makes `c = 0 - 1 = -1`, so the lost unit is recorded.

On the next step, `y = x - c = 1 - (-1) = 2`. At that size, 2 is representable, so it gets added. The compensation turns increments that are each too small to register into occasional ones that do.

The parentheses matter. In real-number algebra, `(t - sum) - y` simplifies to zero, and a compiler that did that would break the algorithm. That's why C compilers must not rearrange it unless you enable `-ffast-math`. JavaScript is safe: ECMA-262 requires IEEE 754 semantics, with no reordering and no extra-precision intermediates.
questions.references:
- [Wikipedia: Kahan summation algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahan_summation_algorithm)
- [David Goldberg: *What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic*](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_goldberg.html)

questions.title: Which of these are real reasons to store money as `NUMERIC`/`DECIMAL` instead of `DOUBLE PRECISION`?

options.text: `NUMERIC` stores decimal digits exactly, so `0.1 + 0.2` really is `0.3`.
`SUM()` over a `DOUBLE PRECISION` column can return different totals for the same rows, because a parallel plan changes the order of addition.
`NUMERIC` arithmetic is slower and its scale is effectively unbounded, which is the price of exactness.
`DOUBLE PRECISION` cannot represent values above one million.
`DOUBLE PRECISION` silently rounds every stored value to two decimal places.

questions.explanation:
PostgreSQL's documentation says it plainly: use `numeric` where exactness matters, especially for money, because the floating-point types are inexact.

People often miss the ordering problem, which follows from the non-associativity in the summation question. `SUM()` doesn't add rows in a fixed order. A parallel plan, a different number of workers, or a new index can change the scan order, and the same query over the same rows can return a total that differs in the last digits. Then your reconciliation job fails now and then, and only in production.

`NUMERIC` avoids both problems by storing base-10 digits and doing exact decimal arithmetic. That has a real cost. It runs in software instead of as a hardware instruction, so it's noticeably slower and takes more space. That's fine for a ledger and wrong for the inner loop of a physics simulation.

The two false options overcorrect. Doubles handle huge values fine, which was never the problem, and they don't round to any fixed number of decimal places.

questions.title: What does `Number.EPSILON` actually measure?

options.text: The gap between `1` and the next double above it, which is 2⁻⁵² ≈ 2.22 × 10⁻¹⁶.
The smallest positive double, about 5 × 10⁻³²⁴.
The largest rounding error any double operation can produce.
The smallest difference between two doubles that still compare unequal.

questions.explanation:
`Number.EPSILON` is the ULP at 1, and that's all it is.

```js
Number.EPSILON === 2 ** -52;   // true
Number.EPSILON;                // 2.220446049250313e-16
1 + Number.EPSILON === 1;      // false, it is the next double up
1 + Number.EPSILON / 2 === 1;  // true, half a step rounds back
```

Each wrong option describes a real quantity, which is why they're tempting. The smallest positive double is `Number.MIN_VALUE`, or 2⁻¹⁰⁷⁴. The largest relative rounding error is half a ULP, or `Number.EPSILON / 2`. And the smallest difference between two doubles depends on their size. Near `1e300`, two neighbouring doubles can differ by 10²⁸⁴.

That last point is why `Number.EPSILON` is so often misused, as the next question shows.

questions.title: Why does `Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON` pass for the tenths but fail for the millions?

options.text: `Number.EPSILON` is the gap at magnitude 1. Near 10⁷ one ULP is about 1.9 × 10⁻⁹, roughly eight million times larger.
The larger pair really does differ by more than one ULP, so they are genuinely different numbers.
`Number.EPSILON` is only meaningful for values below `1`.
`Math.abs` itself loses precision on arguments above `2 ** 20`.

questions.title: What is `Number.MIN_VALUE`?

options.text: The smallest positive value a double can hold, about 5 × 10⁻³²⁴.
The most negative value a double can hold, about −1.8 × 10³⁰⁸.
`Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER`, i.e. −9007199254740991.
Zero, since it is the additive identity and the floor of the number line.

questions.explanation:
It's the smallest positive subnormal, 2⁻¹⁰⁷⁴ ≈ 5 × 10⁻³²⁴, which is greater than zero.

```js
Number.MIN_VALUE;      // 5e-324
Number.MIN_VALUE > 0;  // true
```

The name is misleading. It follows a convention where MIN and MAX describe the range of magnitudes, not the ends of the number line. The most negative double is `-Number.MAX_VALUE`, about −1.797 × 10³⁰⁸.

Starting a running minimum at `Number.MIN_VALUE` is a classic bug. That's a tiny positive number, so every negative value in your data gets ignored. Start with `Infinity` instead. That's also what `Math.min()` returns with no arguments, and for the same reason `Math.max()` returns `-Infinity`.

Values this small are subnormal. Below 2⁻¹⁰²² the implicit leading 1 is dropped, and the significand loses bits as the value gets smaller. That lets values shrink gradually toward zero, at the cost of precision and, on some hardware, a big slowdown.

questions.title: In 32-bit floats, does `0.1 + 0.2` equal `0.3`?

options.text: Yes. With only 24 bits of significand, the three roundings happen to land on the same value.
No. The error is inherent to binary floats and gets worse as precision drops.
No. `Math.fround` returns a double, so the comparison behaves exactly as before.
Yes, but only because `Math.fround` truncates toward zero rather than rounding to nearest.

questions.explanation:
Yes, it's `true`. In single precision, `0.1 + 0.2` and `0.3` are the same float. Convert it back to a double and you get `0.30000001192092896`.

This is the most useful lesson from the whole `0.1 + 0.2` example. The mismatch comes from where the rounding boundaries fall at 53 bits. It isn't a law of binary arithmetic. With 24 bits of significand the grid is coarser, and both sides happen to round to the same point. Single precision isn't more accurate. `0.1` is no more representable in float32 than in float64. There are just fewer values to land on.

So more precision doesn't mean fewer surprises, and "it printed the right answer in my test" proves nothing. For exact decimal work, the only lasting fix is to stop using binary floating point.

About the fourth option: `Math.fround` rounds to nearest, as IEEE 754 requires. Truncation is a different operation and gives a different result.

questions.title: Which rounding mode does IEEE 754 apply to arithmetic results by default?

options.text: Round to nearest, ties to even
Round to nearest, ties away from zero
Round toward zero, i.e. truncate
Round toward negative infinity

questions.explanation:
IEEE 754 uses round to nearest, ties to even (also called banker's rounding) for every arithmetic operation by default, and JavaScript doesn't let you change it.

You can see the tie rule directly. Near 2⁵², doubles are 1 apart and `0.5` is exact, so these sums are real ties:

```js
2 ** 52 + 0.5 === 2 ** 52;        // true, tie, 2**52 is even, so down
(2 ** 52 + 1.5) - 2 ** 52 === 2;  // true, tie, so up to the even 2**52+2
1 + 2 ** -53 === 1;               // true, tie, rounds to the even significand
```

Ties to even is preferred over ties away from zero because it has no bias. Always rounding halves up makes long sums drift upward. Rounding to even goes down about as often as up, so the errors cancel out.

Watch out, though: `Math.round` and `toFixed` don't follow this rule. ECMA-262 defines each of them separately. `Math.round` rounds ties toward positive infinity, so `Math.round(-2.5)` is `-2`, not `-3`. `toFixed` rounds ties away from zero, so `(2.5).toFixed(0)` is `"3"`. That's three different rounding rules in one language.

questions.title: Which of these `NaN` expressions evaluate to `true`?

options.text: `Object.is(NaN, NaN)`
`[NaN].includes(NaN)`
`typeof NaN === "number"`
`NaN === NaN`
`[NaN].indexOf(NaN) === 0`

questions.explanation:
`NaN` splits the same three comparison algorithms as `-0`, but the other way around, so it helps to learn them together.

`NaN === NaN` is `false`. IEEE 754 says `NaN` is unequal to everything, including itself.

`Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is `true`. SameValue overrides the IEEE rule on purpose, so you have a reliable identity check.

`[NaN].includes(NaN)` is `true`, but `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` is `-1`. `includes` uses SameValueZero, while the older `indexOf` uses strict equality, so two array search methods disagree about the same array.

`typeof NaN` is `"number"`, because `NaN` is a double. In fact there are many `NaN` bit patterns: any pattern with all exponent bits set and a non-zero significand.

Compare the two cases. With `-0`, `===` and SameValueZero agree, and `Object.is` differs. With `NaN`, `Object.is` and SameValueZero agree, and `===` differs. No two algorithms agree on both values, which is why the language needs all three.

questions.title: How many iterations does `for (let x = 0; x !== 1; x += 0.1)` run?

options.text: It never ends. After ten steps `x` is `0.9999999999999999`, and it keeps going past `1` forever.
Ten, because `x` reaches exactly `1` on the tenth increment.
Eleven, because the check runs before the increment.
Zero, because `0 !== 1` is evaluated against `-0` and short-circuits.

questions.explanation:
It's an infinite loop. Adding `0.1` ten times gives:

```js
let s = 0;
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) s += 0.1;
s;        // 0.9999999999999999
s === 1;  // false
```

Each `+= 0.1` rounds, the errors add up, and the total misses `1` by one ULP. Every later value misses too, so `x !== 1` stays true forever. The same buildup is why adding `0.1` a million times gives `100000.00000133288` instead of `100000`.

There are two fixes. The more reliable one is to loop over integers and compute the float from them, so errors never build up:

```js
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) doSomething(i / 10);
```

Or use `x < 1` instead of `x !== 1`, so a near miss can't run forever. You still can't be sure whether the last iteration runs, which is why I prefer the integer loop.
questions.references:
- [David Goldberg: *What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic*](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_goldberg.html)
- [0.30000000000000004.com](https://0.30000000000000004.com/)

questions.title: What does `parseInt(0.0000005)` return?

options.text: `NaN`

questions.explanation:
`5`. That's off by a factor of ten million, from a function that shouldn't get a number in the first place.

`parseInt` expects a string. If you pass a number, it converts it to a string first, using the same shortest round-trip printing:

```js
String(0.000005);  // "0.000005"   -> parseInt reads "0"
String(0.0000005); // "5e-7"       -> parseInt reads "5", stops at "e"
```

ECMA-262 switches `Number::toString` to exponential notation below 10⁻⁶, and `String(0.000001)` is still `"0.000001"`, so the cutoff is right there. `parseInt` then reads the leading digits and ignores the rest of the string, including `e-7`.

For the same reason, `parseInt(1e21)` returns `1`. Use `parseInt` to parse strings, with a radix. Use `Math.trunc` to turn a number into an integer. Passing a number to `parseInt` is always a bug, even when it happens to work.

questions.title: Which of these approaches make money arithmetic correct in JavaScript?

options.text: Store amounts as integer minor units, such as cents, and divide only when rendering.
Use an arbitrary-precision decimal library such as `decimal.js` or `big.js`.
Use `BigInt` for the minor units when totals can exceed `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`.
Call `.toFixed(2)` after each arithmetic step to clamp the accumulated error.
Replace `===` with `Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON` throughout.

questions.explanation:
The three that work have one thing in common: the value is never a binary float.

```js
10 + 20 === 30;          // true, integer cents are exact
0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3;       // false, the same amounts as floats
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER; // 9007199254740991 cents, about $90 trillion
```

With integer minor units, `10 + 20 === 30` exactly, because integers below 2⁵³ are exact. The only lossy step is dividing for display, and that happens once, at the end. Stripe's API works this way. Every amount is an integer in the currency's smallest unit.

A decimal library like `decimal.js` or `big.js` does base-10 arithmetic in software, with the same trade-off as SQL `NUMERIC`. You need one for exact fractional values, such as tax rates, per-unit prices, or currencies with three decimal places.

`BigInt` minor units matter once cents go past `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, at about $90 trillion. Most ledgers won't get there, but large aggregates, low-value currencies, or crypto amounts in wei can.

Unfortunately, the two that fail are the popular ones. Calling `toFixed(2)` after every step adds error instead of removing it, because each call rounds again on top of the storage error. And `(1.005).toFixed(2)` shows you can't trust it even once. A tolerance comparison doesn't make the math correct either. It hides the bug, so two ledgers that really differ by a cent compare as equal.

The TC39 Decimal proposal would add exact decimals to the language. It hasn't shipped yet, so for now use one of the three approaches above.
